specPoints.text: use the relationship between energy transferred, current, voltage and time: energy transferred = current × voltage × time

primer.text: When charge is driven around a circuit, the battery is doing work — and work done is energy transferred. This note assembles the three quantities that set the size of that transfer, the current, the voltage and the time in seconds, into the single equation E = I × V × t, and shows it is just power multiplied by time.

lessons.title: Calculating energy transfers
lessons.opening: Charge flowing through a component is the battery doing work on it, and the energy handed over depends on three things: how hard the charge is pushed (voltage), how much flow there is (current) and how long the flow lasts (time). Multiply the three and you have the energy transferred in joules.
keyPoints: Work done by the moving charge equals the energy transferred in the circuit.
Energy transferred depends on the current, the voltage and the time the component runs.
The equation of record is E = I × V × t, with energy in joules.
It is E = P × t with the power written as P = I × V.
Time must enter the equation in seconds, never minutes.
The energy the battery supplies equals the total transferred to every component.

low.restatement: Energy transferred equals current × voltage × time; the longer a device runs, the more energy it moves.
low.analogy: Filling a paddling pool: the flow rate (current), the pressure (voltage) and the filling time together set the water collected.
low.examPointer: Convert minutes to seconds before substituting — this single slip loses the most marks here.

medium.restatement: Because P = I × V, the same law can be read as E = P × t; the two forms are one relationship seen two ways.
medium.analogy: A taxi fare: the rate per mile (power) times the miles driven (time at speed) gives the total paid (energy).
medium.examPointer: 'Work done' and 'energy transferred' are interchangeable in mark schemes — use either name confidently.

check.stem: Charge flowing through a resistor transfers energy that makes the resistor:

options.explanation: The transfer warms the resistor; magnetism is not part of this relationship.
The transferred energy heats the resistor as the charge is pushed through.
Energy transfer does not leave the resistor charged.
The transfer raises, not lowers, the temperature.

check.stem: Energy transferred by electrical work equals:

options.explanation: The current multiplies the voltage; dividing has no meaning here.
That is not any relationship of record.
Time multiplies in — longer running transfers more energy.
E = I × V × t is the relationship of record.

check.stem: A 0.7 A appliance on 4 V runs for one minute. The energy transferred is:

options.explanation: E = 0.7 × 4 × 60 = 168 J, with the minute converted to 60 s.
That is only 0.7 × 4 — the time was dropped.
That is 4 × 60 — the current was dropped.
That used 6 s instead of 60 s.

check.stem: Before substituting into E = I × V × t, any time given in minutes must be:

options.explanation: Leaving minutes overstates nothing consistently — it breaks the joule arithmetic.
Hours move further from the SI unit, not closer.
The joule arithmetic only works with time in seconds.
Halving is not a unit conversion.

check.stem: 'Work done' and 'energy transferred' in circuits are:

options.explanation: They name the same physical quantity.

options.text: two names for the same quantity
options.explanation: Work done by the charge is exactly the energy transferred.
No sign distinction exists in this usage.
Both are measured in joules.

check.stem: State the equation linking energy transferred, current, voltage and time, naming the unit of energy.
check.modelAnswer: E = I × V × t, with energy in joules, current in amperes, voltage in volts and time in seconds.

check.stem: How are E = I × V × t and E = P × t connected?
check.modelAnswer: The power in E = P × t is itself P = I × V, so substituting that into E = P × t gives E = I × V × t.

check.stem: Explain why the time in E = I × V × t must be in seconds.
check.modelAnswer: The watt is one joule per second, so only a time in seconds makes the energy come out in joules; a time left in minutes would understate the transfer by a factor of sixty.

check.stem: A 2 A heater on 12 V runs for 30 s. Calculate the energy transferred.

glossary.definition: The energy handed over by the moving charge, equal to the work done, in joules.
Another name for energy transferred when charge flows around a circuit.

workedExample.prompt: Calculate the energy transferred in 1 minute when a current of 0.7 A passes through a potential difference of 4 V.
steps: List the knowns: time t = 1 minute = 60 s, current I = 0.7 A, potential difference V = 4 V.
State the linking equation: E = I × V × t.
